prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and molecular identity of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate every member placed first, and the reason is substantive rather than a matter of herd behaviour. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide, to receptor agonists with large, independently replicated outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. It combines physiological originality, mechanistic clarity, and very large benefit to patients, and a decade or more of confirmation removes any maturity concern. As a neurologist I also note that the central appetite and neuroprotective actions of GLP-1 signalling are opening further clinical territory. Having listened to colleagues, I now favour a basic-science trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov over my opening trio with Knudsen, because the prize is for physiology or medicine and the discovery to be honoured is the hormone's biology and molecular identity.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited people compete for three places, Mojsov's priority and weighting are contested, and omitted early contributors may matter. Leaving out Knudsen, whose team engineered liraglutide and semaglutide and made the biology a usable medicine, risks reading as if the committee is rewarding the hormone but not the drug-development step that produced the societal impact. A second concern is that a unanimous opening first place can hide quite different views about which part of the story the prize actually honours.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treats Knudsen's industrial role as translation, and ranks optogenetics second as a method with enormous reach for circuit physiology.
responses.response: I now agree with his GLP-1 trio, and I moved toward it from my opening trio with Knudsen. I am more cautious than he is about optogenetics as the fallback. A six-person credit list with serious claims from Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck means any three-person set is open to challenge on attribution, and the clinical payoff is still early. His own note on painful exclusions weakens the case for it as a robust second option.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks GLP-1 first on a basic-science trio, but puts cGAS-STING second and orexin third, preferring mechanism-defining discoveries with clean credit.
responses.response: I share his insistence that the Committee not reward impact alone, and I agree that cGAS-STING has clean two-person credit with Chen and Barber. We differ on ranking: I place it behind CAR-T because STING agonists and inhibitors have not yet shown clinical benefit, so the case is largely mechanistic. I do not think that is disqualifying, and I would be open to pairing it with GLP-1 in a two-part prize if the group wants one. I consider the Chen/Barber attribution tidier than the STING priority question suggests, but I would want that checked.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks GLP-1 first, then the anti-TNF work of Feldmann and Maini, with CAR-T and imatinib near the top, valuing proven clinical transformation with a coherent two- or three-person credit.
responses.response: Her emphasis on proven patient benefit is fair, and it is why I keep CAR-T on my list. I think she is right that clinically transformative therapies with well-defined credit deserve serious weight. I qualify this for CAR-T because the credit list omits Eshhar and other early chimeric-receptor inventors, and solid-tumour results remain limited. Anti-TNF and imatinib are not on the shortlist, so I leave them aside, but the same standard applies: neither clinical impact nor opening support substitutes for a clear scientific discovery with fair attribution.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first, then cGAS-STING and the unfolded protein response, and favours conceptually clean mechanisms with tidy two-person credit such as Walter and Mori.
responses.response: The unfolded protein response is a strong, mature and conceptually clean discovery, and Walter and Mori are a natural pair. I would still not place it ahead of the clinically anchored candidates, because its consequences for disease are mostly indirect. If the Committee wanted a second distinct achievement beside GLP-1, I would consider it on merit. I do not think the three-person limit leaves room for it as a second part unless GLP-1 is cut to one or two people, which I do not favour.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third GLP-1 place, and whether omitted early GLP-1 investigators weaken the credit list.
Whether the Committee prefers a physiology-centred or drug-development-centred award; I have not independently verified priority claims.
Whether optogenetics, CAR-T or cGAS-STING is the better fallback given unresolved attribution in each.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored roughly twenty works with Thomas Perlmann and trained with Paul Greengard, but neither relationship involves any shortlisted candidate. I serve as chair and treat these ties as disclosed context only.
